name: Zoe Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior developer on refrigerated-delivery software at a tech company, after years in cold-store dispatch and a two-year college diploma. I use AI every day to draft tests, but I still check the probe log with a senior engineer. Nik, my partner, repairs shop fridges, our children are grown, and typical developer pay has helped us save five months of expenses while renting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team that small AI gains are useful for spotting a strange temperature reading, but the refrigerated box still needs a working probe. I use AI every day to draft tests for our food-delivery software and compare them with the actual sensor log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58 and a junior developer despite a two-year college diploma, but this tech company pays the usual developer rate. Nik repairs shop fridges, our children are grown, and five months of expenses saved means our rent is covered even when a repair booking slips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep testing the delivery-temperature alerts each morning and ask the senior engineer to review my changes. We would save 100 monthly while both wages arrive and replace the worn kitchen tap from current pay rather than the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about work and rent here. A warm box is a real problem, but the company still needs us to find it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was a bad reading?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A truck probe showed four degrees while the box was warm because the cable was loose. I compared its log with the driver’s handheld thermometer before we warned a grocery shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why are you still junior?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I moved from cold-store dispatch into coding only three years ago. I know the route sheets well, but I still need help with a complicated code change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking planning, checking, buying and coding could write many of my delivery alert tests. I would want a named person to stop a warm load reaching a shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior hours could shrink if one senior can oversee the tests AI writes. Five months saved gives us time, but Nik’s fridge-repair work cannot replace my whole wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my lead for approved paid time to learn the new AI temperature-anomaly tool on old delivery logs. If approved, I’d test a false cold reading each week and document what the tool missed; if my hours fall, I’d search paid local cold-store software vacancies only if their wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my hours but keen to test the tool. I have seen a neat chart hide a box of spoiled food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you catch the false cold reading?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the truck probe with the handheld thermometer and the door-open log. One sensor number is not enough when food is at stake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your lead refuses paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current test work and ask for notice of any hours cut. I would not run the new tool on live loads without approval.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write the delivery code and check temperature logs cheaper than our team. Robots loading food or repairing a fridge might come around 2031, after our screen work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior role could end quickly, though we have five months saved. Nik’s repair jobs may continue for a few more years, but I would not call that a permanent shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d postpone replacing our old sofa and ask for written notice of any developer cuts now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local refrigerated-warehouse checking shifts only if vacancies exist and wages cover rent and bills; I would ask the public employment office what short-term help we qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing my wage before finding a paid shift. Five months of food money is not five months of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the savings to buy a van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not bet our rent reserve on a delivery business when robots may load and carry goods. I would use the savings for our bills while searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a warehouse shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would search the local cold stores and tech firms. Nik’s repair clients are here, and I do not have a paid offer elsewhere.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach delivery code first.
I expect **loading robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **junior wage** could end under fast AGI.
I know **five months saved** is a limited bridge.
do: **Postpone sofa purchase** and request written cut notice now.
**Apply for warehouse checks** after 2028 loss only if local vacancies cover rent and bills.
**Ask public employment office** about actual help eligibility if displaced.
feel: **Alarmed** about lost wage and uncertain shifts.
S2.quote: Five months of food money is not five months of work.
fieldNote: Her **warehouse shift** is a conditional paid bridge before physical robots, not guaranteed lasting work.
She preserves **rent savings** instead of buying a delivery van on speculation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us time to find out whether food firms still need people to check a damaged load. Robots for loading and fridge repair may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn more about actual cold-store inspections while my developer wage lasts, though AGI may plan them too. I would not spend the five-month reserve on a course without a paid opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask a local cold store about a paid weekend checking shift and what food-safety training it funds. If a shift exists, its pay covers travel and the employer funds supervised training, I’d take one each month while my developer job allows outside work; we would save 80 monthly while both wages hold, and if coding ends after 2031 I’d apply for paid local checking vacancies only if wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my code role, but a paid shift would tell me more than a brochure. One warm crate can explain more than a hundred slides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check on that shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the truck log, a handheld temperature reading and the seal on a sample crate under a supervisor. I would not sign a full inspection alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no shift is offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my developer job and savings. I would not claim that asking a cold store taught me inspection work.

I expect **loading robots around 2034** to follow later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 lets us improve the temperature records and save some money. Robots for physical loading and fridge work may come about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still want paid work at 68, and I have not checked a retirement figure. If both wages continue, I could build a longer cushion while testing whether inspection work actually suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep testing cold-chain alerts, save 110 monthly while both wages hold and take paid supervised warehouse shifts if vacancies, travel pay and outside-work approval continue. If my developer role ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local cold-store checking work only where vacancies and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be uneasy about the later job switch but secure in the next few years. The probe cannot promise me a wage, but it can tell me whether I like the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you resign for unpaid training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would keep the developer wage while it exists. I would not resign for a training promise without a paid opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your children’s income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children have their own budgets. Nik and I will make our plan from wages and savings we can see.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my coding wage could end before a paid local warehouse shift exists. Written notice, a real checking vacancy and verified temporary public help would let us use the buffer carefully.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a warehouse shift would be safe forever. Loading robots arrive later, so I need pay and evidence now rather than a promise.

headlineQuote: Loading robots arrive later, so I need pay and evidence now rather than a promise.
portrait: Zoe is a **58-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, typical pay and five months saved.
She and Nik **rent** while their grown children live separately.
She **uses AI daily** but checks cold-chain alerts against probe readings.
She tests **paid warehouse checks** only with vacancy, travel pay, supervised training and outside-work approval.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her coding wage before paid warehouse checking work appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a paid local checking vacancy and verified public support would help.
